claims.text: A sub-5 nm alumina layer will be deposited by atomic layer deposition on the AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy-alloy bond coat.
The ALD process will be performed at approximately 300°C using precursors such as trimethylaluminum and water.
Low-temperature ALD prevents alteration of the underlying HEA microstructure.
The intervention produces a continuous, dense alumina layer between the HEA bond coat and ceramic top coat.
The ultrathin alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier.
The alumina barrier limits interdiffusion of deleterious elements.
Limiting interdiffusion stabilizes both the HEA bond coat and the ceramic top coat.
The ultrathin alumina layer improves adhesion between the bond coat and ceramic top coat.
Improved adhesion reduces delamination during high-temperature thermal cycling.
Improved adhesion reduces oxide-scale spallation during high-temperature thermal cycling.
The ALD-treated system will have greater fatigue resistance than an otherwise comparable system without the ALD barrier.
The ALD-treated system will have a longer service life under cyclic high-temperature conditions than the untreated baseline.
Effectiveness depends on formation of a uniform and dense alumina film.
An incomplete or nonuniform alumina layer could cause the intervention to fail.
Rapid degradation of the alumina barrier during thermal cycling would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity, adhesion, and fatigue life relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
